title: Genetic variant-based drug discovery targeting conserved pathways of aging
text:
Aging is the most important risk factor for human chronic diseases, including type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular
disease, cancer and neurodegeneration. Here we propose to continue our new approach for developing
therapies for these diseases. Rather than focusing on individual diseases, we focus on the genetic differences
between successfully aged, healthy centenarians and control individuals with no family history of extreme
longevity. Based on results from the previous project period, many of such genetic differences involve
physiological processes that have previously been shown to be involved in extreme longevity of model
organisms. Using extensive genetic resources, including whole exome sequences of our ~ 700 centenarians (in
the process of significant expansion), we aim to discover novel genetic variants involved in healthy aging and
longevity. We will then validate these human genetic variants in other centenarian cohorts, subsequently
functionalize the top candidates in vitro and in mice in vivo, and develop drug screening assays for these variants.
This genes-to-drugs collaborative project is the first to use the genetics of the very rare individuals aged over a
hundred in relatively good health to identify therapeutic approaches for targeting aging itself rather than its
composite diseases for preventing, delaying onset and progression, and possibly even reverting many of the
multiple age-related diseases.

title: Integrating patient-reported outcomes and T-cell receptor sequencing to predict immune-related adverse events
text:
Identifying the risk for severe immune-related adverse events will have a major public health impact as risk
assessment-based monitoring will facilitate early detection and prompt management of immune-related ad-
verse events, minimizing the progression to life-threatening or fatal events. Thus, this approach will reduce
treatment-induced symptom burden and mortality, while significantly improving treatment adherence and treat-
ment outcome. This strategy aligns with NCI Cancer Moonshot Blue Ribbon Panel 2016 recommendations to
systematically gather patient-reported outcomes and develop innovative patient-based approaches to facilitate
adherence to effective therapies and improve patients’ quality of life.

title: Combining Separation, Digestion, and Ionization on a Mass Spectrometry Cartridge to Enable Biomedical Research on Proteoforms
text:
Proteoforms, the diverse molecular entities that comprise a protein, can have myriad biological functions and roles in
disease. The most powerful method for proteoform measurement is mass spectrometry, but proteoform measurement
using this instrument tends to be slow and difficult. We aim to develop technologies to enable rapid and simpler
proteoform measurement by mass spectrometry for the purpose of enabling more biomedical research into proteoform
function in biology and human disease.

title: Kids: Nocturnal Investigation into Glomerular Disease, Hypertension, and Transcriptomics (kNIGHT)
text:
The proposed research will further knowledge about the cardiovascular risks, clinical predictors and molecular
markers that drive nocturnal blood pressure dysregulation (nocturnal hypertension and non-dipper status) in
children with proteinuric glomerulopathies. The long-term goal is to guide prevention and treatment for nocturnal
blood pressure dysregulation to meaningfully improve cardiovascular disease outcomes in children with
proteinuric glomerulopathies. The precision medicine approach employed in this study provides an
individualized, patient-oriented approach to nocturnal blood pressure dysregulation, which is critical for the
prevention of future cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in these high-risk children.

title: Non-invasive Imaging of Pathological Fibrin Deposition and its Effect on Progressive Neurodegeneration in the Human Brain: an in vivo longitudinal study
text:
Strong experimental evidence indicates that fibrinogen and its degradation products represent main triggers of
neuroinflammation in a variety of neurological conditions. Despite this compelling evidence, diagnostic and
clinical use of fibrin(ogen) deposition in the human brain beyond rudimentary immunohistochemical detection
on post-mortem samples has not been achieved yet. We propose a multimodal imaging study that will combine
64Cu-FBP8, a novel positron emission tomography probe developed at Massachusetts General Hospital, to
image and quantify in vivo pathological deposition of fibrin in the human brain, with a specific focus on
progressive multiple sclerosis (MS), with quantitative MR protocols at 3 and 7 Tesla MRI, to assess,
longitudinally, the relation between brain fibrin deposition and neurodegeneration.

title: Population genomic inferences of history and selection across populations and time
text:
The proposed research is relevant to public health because understanding natural selection plays a key role in
combating genetic and infectious diseases. The proposed research will generate new methods for identifying
both negative and positive natural selection in natural populations, including humans. These methods will form
a foundation for predicting, for example, rates of adaptation of pathogens and the architecture of human genetic
disease.

title: Rapid, high throughput acquisition of 3D morphology of single cells
text:
Contact PD/PI: LEE, ABRAHAM
Narrative
The 2D morphology of single cells has recently been shown to encode for metastasis propensity of
cancer cells and cellular senescence in fibroblasts and neurons. For this grant, it is expected that 3D
morphology of both the cell membranes and the intracellular organelles will be exponentially more
powerful as a health indicator for early detection of diseases. In addition to precision diagnostics, the
3D morphology of a large population of cells can be gleaned to optimize the engineering of cells for
various therapeutic biologics such as monoclonal antibodies and cell-based therapies.

title: Exposure Signatures Facility Core
text: The Exposure Signatures Facility Core (ESFC) is a consortium of six analytical resources that each contribute unique capabilities to identifying and quantifying toxicants and biological responses to toxicant exposure. High performance technologies including small molecule quantitative analysis, epigenomic, transcriptomic, and proteomic analyses are most frequently requested by CURES Center investigators and form the base for ESFC services. With Center investigators increasingly focused on questions regarding the interaction of environmental exposure and the physiological response to chemical and non-chemical stressors we have included analytical resources to quantify protein and DNA adducts, small molecule toxicants and metabolites, cellular profiling as well as cytokines, lipids and metabolites. Our combined facilities include some of the most advanced analytical capabilities available for targeted and untargeted analysis of the exposome and for discovery of exposure signatures. Although we focus on the common matrices of blood, plasma, urine, cells and tissues, we can work with any biological or environmental sample matrix. Because few investigators are familiar with the full scope and power of the technologies available through the ESFC we consult with investigators as they are planning a project. We offer advice regarding analytical end points, how those end points could be achieved experimentally and the cost involved in doing that work. To offset costs at the initial stages of a study 28 vouchers of $2500 are available each year. Vouchers can be used in any of the six ESFC labs. Investigators are rarely familiar with the latest advances in technology or which is most appropriate for the study. Omics technologies produce data sets that require specialized software available in the laboratory where the data are generated. Using our experience with bioinformatics for interpretation of the data is the final step offered by the ESFC. The complete ESFC package provides investigators with planning, advanced analytical technology, expert technical assistance and informatics.

title: Elucidating conserved structural details and mechanisms regulating herpes viral fusion
text:
40-70% of humans are infected with Herpes Simplex Virus 1 or 2 (HSV-1 or HSV-2), which cause lifelong,
incurable infections; however, the mechanism by which these viruses enter and infect human cells has not yet
been fully defined. While we know which viral proteins are necessary for entry, we lack tools to study them in a
native environment and do not understand how they interact. This application proposes to characterize the
mechanisms that regulate HSV-1 and HSV-2 entry into host cells, thereby identifying new targets for anti-herpes
interventions.

title: Targeting PIM-2 Kinase for Improving Cancer Immunotherapy
text:
Cancer development is associated with immune suppression, and therefore lifting the suppression has
achieved a certain degree of success to effectively treat a proportion of cancer patients. A family of protein
called PIM kinases (1, 2 and 3) plays a prominent role in promoting tumor growth, but our recent study
indicates that one family member (PIM-2) strongly restrains T lymphocyte responses against tumor. In the
current research, we will test how inhibition of PIM-2 kinase promotes immunity against cancer while directly
suppressing tumor growth, which may reveal a novel strategy for effective cancer immunotherapy.

title: A Multidisciplinary Center for Developing Human and Non-human Primate Brain Cell Atlases
text:
We have assembled a multi-institutional collaborative center with the aim of creating a cellular taxonomy of
molecularly defined cell types in the developing human, Rhesus macaque, and marmoset brain. Our project
employs technologies for automated single nucleus and spatially-resolved RNA-sequencing and single cell
transposase accessible chromatin sequencing to create spatial gene expression and epigenomic developmental
expression maps for human and NHP brain. We will sample 30 brain regions at four key epochs of development
and register our cellular data onto MRI-based Common Coordinate Frameworks to create a unique resource that
will serve as a blueprint for studies of human brain function and selective vulnerability of cell types to disease
and will provide foundational data for the development of primate and in vitro models.

title: Application of a Bayesian strategy to ABCD: Identification of substance use risk and COVID-19 effects on neurodevelopment
text:
The Adolescent Brain and Cognitive Development (ABCD) study is a longitudinal study of unprecedented size
and scope, with the potential to transform understanding of the neurobiology of substance-use risk. However,
individuals in this cohort face a unique developmental challenge—entering adolescence during the COVID-19
pandemic. This application leverages recent advances in Bayesian machine learning to carefully delineate
neurodevelopmental trajectories of substance use risk with specific consideration of the societal and individual
effects of COVID-19 using longitudinal data from ABCD (ages 10-14, N>10,000).

title: Rectifying Differences Associated with Risk Score-Based MTM Eligibility in Enhanced MTM
text: This project explores strategies to identify and resolve differences across population groups associated with risk score-based eligibility criteria for medication therapy management (MTM) services in the Enhanced MTM program for Medicare. This project is highly relevant to public health because its long-term goal is to improve health outcomes among the older adult population by reducing differences in medication utilization across population groups. Further, since initiatives by the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services usually spur national changes, our study can exert an impact beyond Medicare.

title: Regulation of Blood Glycoproteins by Lectin Receptors in Health and Disease
text:
Changes in the abundance of circulating blood glycoproteins are important experimental and clinical
determinants of health and disease; however, the mechanisms regulating blood protein half-lives have been
difficult to perceive. We have developed the means to identify the endogenous ligand repertoires of endocytic
lectin receptors that control blood glycoprotein half-lives and by using meta-analyses of the data we can predict
previously undetected phenotypes and disease signs linked to their dysfunction including inflammation,
coagulopathy, cardiovascular defects, and high blood pressure, as well as other physiological effects. This
research proposal will investigate lectin receptor ligand repertoires and functions in blood protein homeostasis
and its potential collaboration with environmental factors in further determining susceptibility to disease.

title: Asian Cohort for Alzheimer's Disease (ACAD)
text: Narrative The ACAD project will build the first major AD genetics study for Asians in US and Canada. Successful completion will lead to new genetic and lifestyle screening markers for Asian Americans and insights about novel therapeutic targets for AD. ACAD will be a first network for recruiting and studying AD in Asian Americans, serving the unmet needs of Alzheimer’s disease research for Asian Americans.

title: Computational Modeling of Ambiguity Aversion in Internalizing Disorders: Neural and Behavioral Markers, and a Test of Target Engagement
text:
As highlighted by the COVID-19 pandemic, ambiguous situations are highly aversive, and exert a powerful
influence on mental health; for example, too much avoidance of or aversion to ambiguity has been tied with
internalizing disorders (e.g., depression and anxiety-related disorders). This project aims to use computational
modeling of decision-making behavior, psychophysiology, and an experimental manipulation to test whether
ambiguity aversion is a behavioral and neural mechanism of internalizing disorders. By using multiple methods,
this study will help clarify whether abnormal levels of ambiguity aversion contribute to internalizing
psychopathology, and how targeted behavioral interventions have the potential to decrease ambiguity aversion.

title: Chemical tools to reveal the sterol lipid interactome in the syphilis agent Treponema pallidum
text:
Syphilis is a sexually transmitted disease caused by bacterial infection of the spirochete Treponema pallidum,
and its prevalence has increased globally in the last decade to contribute to over-prescriptions of antibiotics.
While host cell lipids (including sterols) are critical to the maintenance of the cell envelope of Treponema
pallidum, little is known about the Treponemal proteins that obtain lipids from the host. This project proposes to
identify and biochemically characterize key lipid and sterol interacting proteins in Treponema pallidum to expand
the knowledge of syphilis pathogenesis.

title: Class-Selective Chemical Probes to Resolve Reactive Aldehyde Signaling in Living Systems
text:
Reactive aldehydes are toxic chemical byproducts linked to diabetes, heart disease, and neurodegeneration, yet
current medical tools cannot identify the specific types driving these diseases. This project will develop a first-of-
its-kind toolkit of fluorescent sensors capable of distinguishing four distinct classes of these molecules in living
cells. By pinpointing the exact molecular culprits rather than general damage signals, this research will uncover
new disease mechanisms and guide the development of precise prevention and treatment strategies.

title: Intraoperative Near Infrared Molecular Imaging of Lung Cancer
text:
Once diagnosed with lung cancer, a patient typically undergoes diagnostic bronchoscopy and/or
therapeutic surgery. These procedures carry a 40% failure rate due to missed tumors, positive margins,
un-identified lymph nodes, and synchronous cancers. Our Project will address this problem using near-
infrared optical imaging technology.

title: Homeostasis functions of SKN-1A/Nrf1
text:
The model organism C. elegans has proven to be invaluable for discovery of mechanisms that
influence aging and metabolism. Here we will build upon our recent work in C. elegans to determine how the
master gene regulator SKN-1A/Nrf1 responds to the unsaturated fat oleic acid to benefit the organism and
increase lifespan. We will also determine how stress in the protein synthesis machinery alters metabolism,
and why this gene regulator is then protective, work that will provide fundamental insights into mechanisms
that maintain protein synthesis and may suggest strategies for treating the human genetic disease Diamond-
Blackfan anemia.
